source: Marathon Excellence 18-week web PDF (marathonexcellence.com, imperial), cross-checked against Kindle screenshots; PDF wins on conflicts
recommended_for: First-time marathoners, injury-prone runners, and runners with less than two years of experience; modest time demands, less challenging workouts, and lower injury risk. Uses 2–3-day mini-blocks of higher volume (e.g. ~10 mi/day three days running) that deliver some of the benefits of a 70-mile week and start preparing the body for higher mileage later in a marathon career.
experience: Little or no background in serious training; less than two years of running experience
structural_features: Single daily sessions only (no doubles); 7 running/off days per week
Two peak-mileage variants as parameters (canyon-40 / canyon-50); the first goal-mileage number is the 40 variant, the second the 50 variant
General phase uses % of 5k pace; supportive and specific phases use % of marathon pace (MP)
Kenyan-style progression runs recur through the general phase
Alternating-kilometer sessions at/around MP through weeks 12–17

Key-workout timing: long fast runs at 90–95% MP on Saturdays of weeks 11, 13, 15; marathon-pace sessions in weeks 12, 14, 16 (Saturday) and 17 (Wednesday); midweek specific-speed (105% MP) in weeks 11, 13, 15, 17; supportive-speed (108–112% MP) in weeks 12, 14, 16
Down weeks at weeks 4, 8, and 12 (week 8's down week effectively starts after Tuesday's workout)
A longer race (8k–half marathon) may replace a weekend workout on one or two weekends
All running counts as mileage, including warm-ups, cool-downs, and strides
Peak mileage reached in week 7 (general); week 9 returns to peak before the supportive phase
Specific phase (weeks 15–17) uses mileage ranges so the athlete can adjust within the range to recover after big workouts

sessions.workout: 5 mi Kenyan-style progression run + 0.5 mi easy cool-down

1 mi progressive warm-up + 4 strides
10 × 1.5 min at 100% 5k with 1 min jog
0.5 mi easy cool-down

weeks.notes: Early weeks are for learning pacing through Kenyan-style progression runs — start extremely easy and focus on running fast but relaxed in the second half; fading late from starting too eagerly is a normal part of learning. Wednesday's 10 × 1.5 min at 100% 5k is the first check on the fitness estimate — if it feels too hard, the 5k pace estimate is too optimistic. "Easy progressing to moderate" means roughly 50–60% 5k pace early, dropping to about 65–75% 5k pace for the second half when feeling good; stay strictly easy when fatigued. This week and next week's long runs are "time on feet" — fatigue should come from duration, not intensity. Saturday's hills can be modest: a few 40–100 ft climbs totaling 200–600 ft is plenty.

sessions.workout: 5 mi Kenyan-style progression run + 0.5 mi easy cool-down

1 mi progressive warm-up + 4 strides
4 mi at 85% 5k
0.5 mi easy cool-down

weeks.notes: Wednesday's strong run should feel strong but controlled — definitely backed off from half-marathon pace; even at the end you should feel you could easily do another mile or two at the same pace with no real fatigue accumulating. Strides are about smoothness and efficiency — emphatically not sprints. At week's end, do a quick review of the last few weeks' workouts and revise the fitness estimate if needed: if you're hitting paces and perceived difficulty matches the targets, keep the estimate as-is; otherwise adjust up or down.

sessions.workout:
1.5 mi progressive warm-up + 4 strides
6–7 × 3 min at 90% 5k with 1 min jog
0.5 mi easy cool-down

1.5 mi progressive warm-up + 4 strides
8 × 2 min at 100% 5k with 1.5 min jog
0.5 mi easy cool-down

1 mi progressive warm-up + 4 strides
9 mi at 70–75% 5k
No cool-down

weeks.notes: Monday's cruise intervals are a classic "threshold workout" — fast but relaxed, with no fatigue accumulating from rep to rep; adjust the rep count so you finish feeling you could do a few more at the same pace. Wednesday's intervals are the logical next step from week 1's 10 × 1.5 min — pace them evenly both rep to rep and within each rep; don't start fast and fade in the second minute. Saturday is the first long fast run of the buildup: you may get uncomfortable late, but it shouldn't be overly tough; pace may bounce around, and anything in the 70–75% 5k range is fine.

sessions.workout: 5–6 mi easy to moderate with 4 × 20 sec strides

1 mi progressive warm-up + 4 strides
5 mi at 85% 5k
No cool-down
6 mi Kenyan-style progression run + 1 mi easy cool-down

weeks.notes: First down week — reduced mileage and only two workouts; use it to freshen up and consolidate fitness gains. Wednesday's strong run extends to 5 mi at 85% 5k — hold the same pace longer, aiming to feel after five miles the way you did after four last time. Saturday's progression run grows a mile too — add it "in the middle," lengthening the strong high-end-aerobic stretch before dropping the pace over the last 1–1.5 mi. Revise the fitness estimate after this week: recent workouts at 85/90/100% 5k pace are the best guide, plus the fastest mile of your progression runs (runners at this level typically close the last mile at 90–92% of current 5k pace).

sessions.workout:
1.5 mi progressive warm-up + 4 strides
7–8 × 3 min at 90–92% 5k with 45 sec jog
1 mi easy cool-down

1.5 mi progressive warm-up + 4 strides
3 × (3 min at 100% 5k, 1.5 min jog, 2 min at 102% 5k, 3 min jog)
1 mi easy cool-down

weeks.notes: Monday's cruise intervals add a rep and widen the pace range; now that high-end-aerobic work is familiar, explore a slightly faster pace and watch for any abrupt rise in fatigue — the shorter 45-sec recovery keeps pacing honest. Wednesday is a mixed-pace session just above 5k pace: don't chase a perfect number on the 2-min repeats; each one only needs to be a bit faster than the preceding 3-min rep (101% or 104% both deliver the effect). The long run is long enough to tire you late — that fatigue should come from duration and hills, never intensity.

sessions.workout:
1.5 mi progressive warm-up + 4 strides
2 sets of (6 × 500m at 95% 5k with 30 sec walk), with 4 min walk between sets
1 mi easy cool-down

1.5 mi progressive warm-up + 4 strides
6 mi at 85% 5k
0.5 mi easy cool-down
7 mi Kenyan-style progression run + 1 mi easy cool-down

weeks.notes: Monday introduces 95% 5k pace — near 8k–10k pace; don't let the short reps fool you, the very short rest gives them the cumulative effect of longer reps; run it as if the between-sets recovery didn't exist (steady moderate intensity throughout), and walk the recoveries — don't jog them. Wednesday's 6 mi strong run should feel like the 5-mi one from two weeks ago — finish feeling you could do another mile or two; aim for even to slightly negative splits, starting controlled and working into it. Saturday's progression run grows another mile — start very easy, work down to a strong but relaxed high-end-aerobic pace in the middle, and close the last 1–1.5 mi faster, finishing feeling you could do one more mile about ten seconds faster.

sessions.workout:
1.5 mi progressive warm-up + 4 strides
4–5 × 5 min at 90–92% 5k with 1 min jog
1 mi easy cool-down

1.5 mi progressive warm-up + 4 strides
7 × 1 km at 95% 5k with 2 min jog
1 mi easy cool-down

1 mi progressive warm-up + 4 strides
11–12 mi at 75–80% 5k
No cool-down

weeks.notes: Cruise intervals like Monday's should feel fast and free-flowing by now — extending the rep to 5 min should pose no real challenge; find the right effort and lock onto it. Wednesday's 1 km repeats extend the 95% 5k distance up from 500m — effort should feel near 8k–10k pace: intense enough to feel some fatigue accumulating, but not like a hard 100% 5k session. Saturday pushes distance and optionally intensity versus your last long fast run — start at 75% 5k, and only if feeling good push down to 80% 5k from halfway; don't push hard early, you'll still have several miles to go at the midpoint. This is the first week at peak mileage — some fatigue and soreness is no surprise; even if it bleeds into workouts, it's no cause for alarm. In the general phase the aim is a high overall training load, not top-quality individual workouts — as long as the effort is right, you're moving in the right direction.

sessions.workout: 4–6 mi very easy with 4 × 20 sec strides

1.5 mi progressive warm-up + 4 strides
3 sets of: (3 min at 98% 5k, 1 min jog, 3 min at 100–102% 5k, 4 min walk/jog)
1 mi easy cool-down

weeks.notes: Tuesday is your chance to test your limits if you've been craving a tougher interval session — three "couples" of 2 × 3 min, where the short jog between lets you push the second 3-min rep of each set (versus running 6 min straight); even pushing to 9/10, do it mostly on the second rep and keep the first rep on the controlled side of 5k pace. This is another down week, though it really starts after Tuesday — the rest of the week is shorter, easier, with no other real workouts; use the lower volume to regenerate and freshen up. If you're really itching for more quality and feeling good, Friday can become a Kenyan-style progression run, but usually an easy-to-moderate run is right. Saturday's long run is a good first chance to practice gels or sports drinks (not strictly required — the pace is easy enough that carb reliance is low). Tuesday's interval paces will help revise your fitness estimate at week's end, alongside how weeks 6 and 7 went.

sessions.workout:
1.5 mi progressive warm-up + 4 strides
4–5 sets of (1200m at 90–92% 5k, 400m at 75% 5k)
1 mi easy cool-down
6 mi Kenyan-style progression run + 1 mi easy cool-down

1.5 mi progressive warm-up + 4 strides
5–6 × 2 km at 86–88% 5k with 2 min walk
1 mi easy cool-down

weeks.notes: Tuesday is the first float-recovery session — it looks like cruise intervals, but the "recovery" still runs at a good clip; use a track if available, otherwise a flat uninterrupted loop with 0.4 km auto-laps so pacing feedback is frequent for both reps and floats. Keep Thursday's progression run controlled (no harder than 7/10) — Tuesday and Saturday are both big sessions, so a lower-intensity midweek effort balances the week. Saturday is high-volume intervals at a slightly faster pace than a traditional strong run — think of it as a strong run broken into short segments rather than a classic interval workout; aim for six reps, five if the week's volume has fatigued your legs; at 86–88% 5k (just slower than half-marathon pace) you shouldn't feel fatigued from the intensity itself.

sessions.workout: 4–7 mi very easy with 4 × 20 sec strides

1.5 mi progressive warm-up + 4 strides
4 × 1.5 km at 95% 5k with 3–4 min jog
1 mi easy cool-down

1 mi progressive warm-up + 4 strides
7–8 mi at 85% 5k
No cool-down

weeks.notes: Tuesday's 95% 5k intervals should feel controlled — near 8k–10k pace, starting closer to 10k pace and working down toward 8k pace if feeling good. Thursday's strong run at 85% 5k grows again; some carryover fatigue is normal, but always finish feeling you could do another mile at the same pace. Keep Saturday's long run strictly easy — a "time on feet" session laying groundwork for future long fast runs; for more challenge use bigger hills or the high end of the distance range, never a faster pace.

sessions.workout:
1.5 mi progressive warm-up + 4 strides
3–4 sets of: (1600m at 90–92% 5k, 400m at 75% 5k)
1 mi easy cool-down
6 mi Kenyan-style progression run with optional fast finish + 1 mi easy cool-down

1 mi progressive warm-up + 4 strides
15–16 mi at 90–92% MP
No cool-down

weeks.notes: The marathon-supportive phase begins. Tuesday continues the 1200m/400m float-recovery session from two weeks ago — same paces, 1600m per set instead of 1200m; aim for four sets, stopping after three if difficulty gets out of control. On Thursday, feel it out coming off the float-recovery workout — if fresh, break from the usual controlled finish and attack the last mile of the progression run to see how fast you can close; only do the fast finish if you feel good, otherwise stay controlled throughout. Midweek you must convert your 5k fitness estimate into a marathon-pace estimate before Saturday: last week's strong run (7 mi at 85% 5k) and week 7's long fast run (11–12 mi at 75–80% 5k) are the two most helpful references; compare how you felt to judge whether marathon pace sits closer to 80% or 85% of 5k pace (81% 5k is a good default, adjustable a few points either way by how training has gone). Don't think of 100% MP as 26.2-mile pace yet — think of it as the fastest pace you could sustain for roughly 15–16 miles in a really tough workout. Saturday's long fast run should feel quite controlled — never too fast to hold for a few more miles, even at the end; start at 90% MP and progress to 92% if feeling good.

sessions.workout:
1.5 mi progressive warm-up + 4 strides
2 sets of (2 km at 108% MP, 1 km at 112% MP) with 3 min jog within sets and 4 min jog between sets
1 mi easy cool-down

1 mi progressive warm-up + 4 strides
8–9 × (1 km at 100–102% MP, 1 km at 85% MP)
1 mi very easy cool-down

weeks.notes: The weekly structure now shifts from the general phase's continually high load to bigger workouts with more recovery afterward — a welcome break after weeks of tough, consistent training. Wednesday's 2 km repeats run at roughly 10k effort with the 1 km repeats closer to 5k pace (controlled side); pacing perfection matters less than even 2 km reps and 1 km reps that are noticeably but not wildly faster. Saturday's alternating kilometers are your first extended look at 100% MP — note the recovery kilometer is still a steady pace, so watch your splits on the floats; late in the workout you can "explore" 101–102% MP to test whether it feels comfortable or too fast, but don't get ambitious — the fast recovery leaves little room for pacing mistakes. Do it on a flat route even if your race is hilly, and take at least two gels during fast kilometers (mostly practice; no need for a high fueling rate yet).

sessions.workout: 4–6 mi easy progressing to moderate with 4 × 20 sec strides

1.5 mi progressive warm-up + 4 strides
7 × (1 km at 105% MP, 1 km at 80% MP)
1 mi easy cool-down

1 mi progressive warm-up + 4 strides
16–18 mi at 90–92% MP
No cool-down

weeks.notes: Wednesday resembles last weekend's alternating kilometers but is really a descendant of the general phase's 1600m/400m float-recovery cruise intervals — fast kilometers near half-marathon effort, recovery kilometers at a still-moderate effort (easier than last weekend's floats, but not easy). Saturday is a true long fast run: simple on paper, equally mental and physical, training you to hold a steady rhythm for hours; run it on race-like terrain, challenging but controlled enough to feel you could do another mile or two if pushed. Take at least three gels (miles 5, 10, 15 suit most runners; the last is mostly practice). If Saturday feels too hard, your fitness estimate is likely too ambitious — when revising the marathon-pace estimate after this week, weight this long fast run and the last few weeks' alternating-kilometer sessions most.

sessions.workout:
1.5 mi progressive warm-up + 4 strides
(3 × 2 km at 108% MP with 4 min jog); then at the end, 1 km at 110–112% MP
1 mi easy cool-down

1 mi progressive warm-up + 4 strides
7 × (2 km at 100% MP, 1 km at 85% MP)
0.5 mi easy cool-down

weeks.notes: Wednesday's 2 km repeats at 108% MP are the main focus; the closing fast kilometer can be a controlled finish or a deliberate push to about 8.5/10 depending on how you feel physically and mentally. Saturday's alternating kilometers are a key marathon-pace dial-in session — visualize racing, fine-tune pacing by whether the pace feels sustainable, and practice your mid-race fueling rate (gels on reps 2, 4, 6 is a common pattern); run the first half flat and the second half on race-specific terrain, and wear super shoes.

sessions.workout:
1.5 mi progressive warm-up + 4 strides
3.5–5 mi at 105% MP
1 mi easy cool-down

1 mi progressive + 4 strides
6 mi at 88% MP, 5 mi at 90% MP,
5 mi at 92% MP, 3–4 mi at 95% MP
No cool-down

weeks.notes: The marathon-specific phase begins: everything now focuses on executing the weekend sessions and recovering well after them — midweek work gets less intense and days after big workouts are very easy. Wednesday's fast continuous run at 105% MP is 3.5–5 mi by feel; use half-mile auto-splits so you can adjust length mid-run, and don't worry if lingering fatigue from last weekend makes it feel a touch harder. Saturday's 19–20 mi step-wise long fast run is probably the toughest session in the plan — start controlled since most of the benefit is in the second half; cap it at 9/10 if possible (9.5 is acceptable to hit pace late), use race-day fueling on race-specific terrain, then recover with high-carb meals and sleep. Adjust mileage within the week's range to feel recovered. Update the fitness estimate after this week — it now provisionally equals goal marathon pace, and every remaining workout keys off race-day pace.

sessions.workout:
1.5 mi progressive warm-up + 4 strides
10–12 × 500m at 108–110% MP with 30–45 sec walk
1 mi easy cool-down

1 mi progressive warm-up + 4 strides
5 km at 98–100% MP, 1 km easy (65–75% MP)
4 km at 100% MP, 1 km easy
3 km at 100% MP, 1 km easy
2 km at 100–102% MP, 1 km easy
1 km at 101–102% MP
0.5 mi easy cool-down

weeks.notes: After last weekend, expect lingering soreness for a few days — keep easy runs easy and accept that easy pace will be significantly slower while recovering from a big workout. Wednesday's 500m repeats should feel quite controlled; it may take a few reps to shake out the soreness, then the intensity should feel almost threshold-like even though the pace is closer to 8k–10k pace; end well before it gets difficult, adjusting reps and recovery as needed. Saturday's workout simulates the race's structure: open the 5 km segment the way you'll open the race (even-paced or progressive start), run the 4 km and 3 km segments as smoothly as possible like the middle miles, then practice pushing the pace in the final 2 km and 1 km while noticing what it feels like to exceed marathon pace slightly — something to watch for on race day. Between-segment recovery is 1 km easy (exact pace not critical). Do it on race-specific terrain in race-day gear, and fuel before and during exactly as you will in the marathon.

sessions.workout:
1.5 mi progressive warm-up + 4 strides
5 × (1 km at 103% MP, 1 km at 85% MP)
1 mi easy cool-down

1 mi progressive warm-up + 4 strides
3–4 × 2 mi at 100% MP with 2–3 min jog
0.5 mi easy cool-down

weeks.notes: The wider mileage range continues so you can fully recover from last weekend's marathon-specific session — keep easy days easy and get enough sleep. Wednesday's alternating kilometers are the last "real" workout before the marathon, and even it should feel a bit on the short side; if still beat up from last weekend, move it to Thursday and swap Saturday's workout for a 7–8 mi easy-to-moderate run — freshness for this session is the priority. The float recovery is now 85% MP (up from 80% in week 13) — the real focus is feeling like you can recover at 85% MP, not hitting the fast kilometers perfectly. Saturday is one more chance to practice marathon pace consistently — it should not be hard, just the first part of a much longer workout; do three reps if fatigued or sore, four if marathon-pace workouts have been hard to pace.

sessions.workout:
1.5 mi progressive warm-up + 4 strides
5–6 × 3 min at 103–106% MP with 1 min jog
1 mi easy cool-down
Off or 4–6 mi very easy to easy

1 mi progressive warm-up + 4 strides
Marathon race

weeks.notes: Race week is deliberately simple — nothing new, one light workout, and short easy runs so you arrive at the start line feeling good. Wednesday should be very controlled, like the first half or two-thirds of a "real" workout; don't be alarmed if the top of the pace range feels quick — marathon-tuned fitness makes faster paces feel more intense than usual; if so, hold 105% MP. The recommended taper stays at the higher end of the easy-run mileage ranges, treating race day like a very tough marathon-specific workout; prefer a more aggressive taper and you'll use the shorter ends of the ranges instead. On race day there are no miracles — just execute what you've practiced in the marathon-specific workouts. If your race is Saturday, skip Monday's session and shift the entire week back one day.
